response:
Diagnosis. Gen 5 resolved the alpha/FMB tension. The winning template is additive SUMRANK pairing the net short-term funding gap with a *second-moment or downside-state* quality leg: VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap now leads on every metric jointly (fmb -2.46, alpha -6.1%, t=-4.91, Sharpe -0.232) and TroughCoverageFundingGapAdditive is second (fmb -2.33, alpha -4.6%). Two negative results also sharpen the search: industry neutralization did not lift the FMB slope and cut the Sharpe by half (-0.080), so I abandon it; and working-capital intensity change was a null (-1.0% alpha, fmb 0.05), so the accrual-style working-capital channel is dead. Remaining questions worth the last generations: (i) can the two best legs be combined without dilution, (ii) is it revenue instability or a demand *drawdown* that carries the effect, (iii) is instability specific to the top line or generic to the cost base, and (iv) which funding-gap normalization and window length is right, given the leader has the archive's lowest coverage (0.101).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: FundingGapWithInstabilityAndTroughCoverage
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act), SUMRANK(VOL(GROWTH(revt, 1), 3), NEG(RATIO(TS_MIN(ADD(pi, dp), 3), lt))))
HYPOTHESIS: Fragility is the joint product of a withdrawable funding structure, an unpredictable revenue stream, and thin worst-case cash coverage of obligations; the funding gap deserves the largest weight because it is the proximate trigger, while instability and trough coverage each supply independent information about whether a shock will arrive and whether it can be absorbed.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The nesting deliberately gives the funding gap 50% and the two conditioning channels 25% each, which matches the evidence that the gap is the common leg of the archive's two highest-alpha signals while the instability and trough-coverage legs are the only ones that have delivered |FMB t| above 2. Because the three legs come from the financing mix, the revenue process and the earnings trough, their measurement errors are largely independent, so the composite should improve the cross-sectional slope without giving up the -5% to -6% alpha magnitude.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: RevenueDrawdownWithFundingGap
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(TS_MAX(revt, 3), revt), revt), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act))
HYPOTHESIS: What threatens a short-funded firm is not symmetric revenue variability but an actual decline from its recent peak: operating in a demand hole while creditors can withdraw funding forces asset sales or dilution, so peak-relative revenue shortfall combined with the funding gap should predict low returns.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This separates the downside from the dispersion interpretation of the archive's best signal — volatility rewards firms that swing upward as much as those that collapse, whereas a drawdown measure is one-sided and directly identifies firms currently below their demonstrated capacity. It is also cheaper in data than a volatility estimate over growth rates, so coverage should improve on the 0.101 of the current leader while testing a genuinely different economic state.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: FundingGapInCostMonthsWithTopLineVol
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(VOL(GROWTH(revt, 1), 3), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), cogs))
HYPOTHESIS: The funding gap is best expressed in operating time — short-term debt net of cash measured in months of operating cost — because that states how long the firm can run if the debt cannot be rolled, whereas scaling by current assets confounds the gap with balance-sheet composition.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This isolates a single design choice, the denominator of the archive's most productive distress leg, holding the instability partner fixed, so any change in the FMB slope or Sharpe is attributable and directly usable in the final generations. Cost-base normalization is also less mechanically related to the current-asset composition legs already tested, which should reduce overlap with the liquidity-composition results.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: RecentGrowthShockWithFundingGap
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(ABS(GROWTH(revt, 1)), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act))
HYPOTHESIS: A large absolute revenue move in either direction is a one-year proxy for an unsettled business — rapid expansion strains working capital while sharp contraction destroys coverage — so pairing it with the funding gap should capture most of the instability effect using only one lag of data.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The current leader sacrifices about three percentage points of coverage to estimate a three-year volatility, and this tests whether that cost is necessary or whether a contemporaneous shock magnitude carries the same information at the archive's maximum coverage. If the alpha and slope survive at higher coverage, the final generation should build on the cheap version; if they collapse, persistent instability rather than a single shock is what matters.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: CostBaseInstabilityWithFundingGap
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(VOL(GROWTH(cogs, 1), 3), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act))
HYPOTHESIS: If the instability that matters is genuine business-model uncertainty, it should show up on the input side too: firms whose operating cost base swings unpredictably face uncertain cash needs, and short-term creditors will not reliably fund those needs.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Run against Signal 3 and the archived revenue-volatility leader, this decomposes the instability channel into demand-side and cost-side components, telling us whether the effect is about unpredictable sales or unpredictable cash requirements. The distinction matters economically because only the cost-side version implies a treasury/working-capital forecasting failure, and it is the version least overlapping with the published information-uncertainty literature built on sales and earnings variability.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: IlliquidOperatingCapitalWithVolatileDemand
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(VOL(GROWTH(revt, 1), 3), RATIO(SUB(wcap, che), cogs))
HYPOTHESIS: Non-cash working capital — inventory and receivables measured in months of operating cost — is capital that cannot be mobilised quickly at full value; a firm holding a large illiquid operating stock while its demand is volatile faces markdown and collection losses precisely when it needs cash.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This tests whether the instability effect requires the financing-side gap at all, or whether illiquid operating capital is an equally good conditioning variable, which distinguishes a creditor-withdrawal mechanism from an asset-liquidation mechanism. Subtracting cash from working capital makes the leg a pure inventory-and-receivables measure rather than a repackaged liquidity ratio, and scaling by the cost base keeps it in interpretable operating-time units.
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel

---CRITIQUE FundingGapWithInstabilityAndTroughCoverage---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The nested weighting is internally consistent and combines the three legs that actually carried the archive's cross-sectional and portfolio evidence, but it is fundamentally a mechanical ensemble of two already-tested composites sharing the same dominant leg, so incremental information is likely modest.

---CRITIQUE RevenueDrawdownWithFundingGap---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: Replacing symmetric growth dispersion with a one-sided peak-relative shortfall is a substantively different economic state (demand hole versus uncertainty), the sign direction matches the expression, and it is not a rediscovery of an archived or standard published anomaly, though the ratio's denominator (revt) will be unstable for very small-revenue firms.

---CRITIQUE FundingGapInCostMonthsWithTopLineVol---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a pure denominator swap (act to cogs) on the archived leader with the partner leg held fixed — a cosmetic scaling variant rather than a new mechanism, and the claim that it reduces overlap with liquidity-composition results is weak since dlc−che dominates either normalization.

---CRITIQUE RecentGrowthShockWithFundingGap---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: Shortening the archived leader's 3-year volatility to a one-year absolute growth is a lag-window variant, and the symmetric |growth| leg conflates the well-known asset/sales-growth anomaly (high growth → low returns) with the intended instability channel, so a confirming result would be uninterpretable.

---CRITIQUE CostBaseInstabilityWithFundingGap---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: COGS growth is nearly collinear with revenue growth for most firms, so this is a near-duplicate of the archived VolatileTopLineWithFundingGap leader dressed in a cost-side story, and the stated demand-versus-treasury decomposition cannot be identified from two such correlated volatility measures.

---CRITIQUE IlliquidOperatingCapitalWithVolatileDemand---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The expression is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis — SUB(wcap, che) equals non-cash current assets *minus current liabilities*, not "inventory and receivables," so high values indicate a conservatively funded working-capital position whose natural return direction is the opposite of the stated negative sign (and contradicts the archived NEG(wcap/at) result).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: NearTermClaimCoverageWithVolatileDemand
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), lct)), VOL(GROWTH(revt, 1), 3))
HYPOTHESIS: The binding constraint within the next year is whether one year of cash earnings can meet the claims actually falling due — payables, accruals and current debt alike — and that mismatch is decisive when revenue is too unpredictable for creditors and suppliers to extend terms.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: This changes the distress leg rather than its scaling: instead of the debt-specific net funding gap it uses cash-earnings coverage of the entire near-term claim stack, which tests whether the archive's effect is a creditor-withdrawal phenomenon or a broader claim-timing mismatch that includes trade and accrued obligations. The construction is a genuine mechanism substitution with the instability partner held fixed, so the comparison against the archived leader is interpretable and both legs remain coverage-friendly.
REASONING_NOTE: none

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: EarningsDownsideAsymmetryWithFundingGap
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(SUB(MA(RATIO(pi, revt), 3), TS_MIN(RATIO(pi, revt), 3)), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act))
HYPOTHESIS: Firms differ in how far their margins fall in a bad year relative to their normal margin, and it is this downside gap — not symmetric variability and not the level of profitability — that determines whether a short-funded firm survives a shock.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: novel
REASONING: The leg is a level-free downside-dispersion measure (mean minus trough margin), so it is orthogonal to the profitability anomaly and distinguishable from both the symmetric volatility leg in the archived leader and the trough-level leg tested in gen 5, directly answering whether dispersion or asymmetry carries the effect. It also avoids the growth-anomaly contamination of an absolute-growth proxy, since a firm can be fast growing and still have a small mean-to-trough margin gap.
REASONING_NOTE: none

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: ChronicTaxDrySpellWithFundingGap
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(txt, revt), 3)), RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), act))
HYPOTHESIS: A firm that has remitted almost no cash tax per dollar of revenue for three consecutive years has persistently generated no taxable income, an externally verified indication that its reported earning power is weak, and such a firm cannot support a funding structure that must be rolled each year.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Cost-of-goods volatility was correctly identified as collinear with revenue volatility, so instead of a duplicate instability leg this substitutes an independent information source — the tax authority's implicit assessment of profitability — smoothed over three years to capture chronic rather than transitory non-payment. Earlier tax legs were paired with balance-sheet leverage and produced modest alphas; pairing chronic tax dryness with the archive's strongest distress leg tests whether the tax channel adds information where leverage did not.
REASONING_NOTE: none

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: InventoryHeavyWithShortTermDebt
EXPRESSION: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, che), cogs), RATIO(dlc, act))
HYPOTHESIS: Non-cash current assets — inventory and receivables expressed in months of operating cost — can only be converted to cash at a discount and with delay, so a firm financing a large illiquid operating stock with short-term debt is exposed to a forced-liquidation loss if that debt is not rolled.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: This corrects the previous specification error: SUB(act, che) is unambiguously non-cash current assets rather than a net working-capital position, so the leg now measures operating-asset illiquidity as intended and its sign no longer contradicts the archived wcap result. Pairing it with short-term debt as a share of the current-asset base isolates an asset-liquidation mechanism that is distinct from the cash-shortfall mechanism dominating the archive, since a firm can have ample cash flow yet still be unable to monetise its stock quickly.
REASONING_NOTE: none
